extracted.intended_audience: science journalists and editors (particularly those at Science News)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practices for reporting and producing science news stories, including newsworthiness criteria, sourcing practices, embargo handling, and quality checks to avoid common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: New findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Original research published in peer-reviewed journals is considered newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize reporting on original research; verify publication venue and whether the research represents new results rather than reanalysis or commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: New techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological breakthroughs or novel techniques merit coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the technique materially changes how research is done or opens new lines of inquiry; explain the technique clearly for non-specialist readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprising statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterintuitive or striking statistical results are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize surprising numbers (sample size, effect size, uncertainty) and avoid sensationalizing isolated figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latest science trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Emerging fields or developing trends in science qualify as newsworthy topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate individual studies within broader trends; look for accumulating evidence and expert commentary to demonstrate a genuine trend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple, appropriate sources: authors of papers, experts cited in the work, independent experts, trusted contacts, and expert recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check claims with independent experts; cultivate and rely on trusted contacts built over time; prioritize primary sources (paper authors) and independent validation rather than press materials alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargo system
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect embargoes that forbid publication until a set time so reporters can prepare thorough coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use embargo time for interviews, expert consultation, and careful reporting; embargoes aim to give fair access to journalists, but be aware of critiques that embargos can make reporting reactive rather than enterprising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review status checked
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm whether research has undergone peer review before treating it as established evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the peer-review status prominently; treat preprints, conference abstracts, and non–peer-reviewed reports with caution and explicit labeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report sample size
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the sample size used in the study being covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sample size as part of contextualizing the study’s reliability and generalizability; when relevant, explain how sample size affects confidence in results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly report and explain the limitations of the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include methodological caveats, scope limits, and any uncertainties; avoid overgeneralizing results beyond what the study supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Report any conflicts of interest disclosed by authors or evident from affiliations/funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate funding sources and author affiliations; disclose meaningful conflicts to readers as part of transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single-study hype
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid hyping single studies without situating them in the broader evidence base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide context by referencing prior work, replication status, and expert views; explicitly warn readers when findings are preliminary or isolated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of finding
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which a finding is new or advances knowledge is an important newsworthiness criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the finding truly advances or changes understanding versus incremental confirmation; seek expert judgment on novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the underlying study’s methods for rigor and appropriateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine study design, controls, blinding, statistical methods, and potential biases; report methodological strengths and weaknesses plainly to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical and practical significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider both statistical significance and real-world (practical) significance of results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report p-values or confidence intervals where relevant, but also explain effect sizes and practical implications for non-specialist readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replicability assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the replicability or reproducibility prospects of the finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note whether findings have been replicated, whether data/code are available, and whether methods permit independent verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprising / counter-expected results
rubrics_metrics.description: Results that contradict expectations or prevailing wisdom are newsworthy if credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat counterintuitive results with scrutiny: check for methodological artifacts, statistical flukes, or alternative explanations; seek independent expert validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health relevance for non-specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether findings have direct health implications that are relevant to general audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid giving premature health advice; require stronger evidence and clear guidance from health experts before presenting findings as actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider and report potential implications of findings for policy or public decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between direct, evidence-based policy relevance and speculative implications; consult policy experts when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful / elegant experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-designed, elegant experimental work can be considered newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain what makes an experiment elegant (clarity of design, clever controls) and why that matters for the result’s credibility or interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputable journal / institution
rubrics_metrics.description: The standing of the publishing journal or institution contributes to newsworthiness and credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the venue of publication and institutional affiliations as contextual cues; do not treat venue alone as proof of quality—combine with methodological assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: The reputation and track record of study authors factor into evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider authors’ histories and prior work, but avoid undue deference; use reputation alongside independent expert assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of voices in science
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek diversity in expert voices (gender, race, geography) when sourcing and presenting science stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make active efforts to include diverse perspectives and avoid over-reliance on a narrow set of experts or institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent expert validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain independent expert comment to cross-check authors’ claims and interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer independent experts unconnected to the study for verification and to explain broader context; document any disagreements among experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overhyping single studies (pitfall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overstate the importance of single studies or present them as definitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide context, note limitations, and avoid headlines or leads that exaggerate certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid implying causation from correlation (pitfall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not suggest causal relationships when the study only demonstrates association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about study design (observational vs. experimental) and explain what conclusions are warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature health advice (pitfall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from issuing or amplifying health recommendations based on preliminary or limited evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult clinical or public-health experts before presenting health advice; emphasize uncertainty when evidence is weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid press-release stenography (pitfall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not copy or uncritically repeat press-release language without independent reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify press-release claims with independent sources and add critical context rather than repeating promotional framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid echo chamber of 'knowns' (pitfall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid recycling the same perspectives or relying only on familiar experts, which can create an echo chamber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively seek diverse and independent viewpoints to challenge consensus and surface blind spots.
